Structured data has been the last domain where foundation models mostly did not apply. Language and vision were rewritten by pretraining; the relational database underneath the business was left alone, still served by per-task models, weeks of feature engineering and hand-tuned pipelines. NVIDIA's **Kumo Relational** is an attempt to close that gap, and the reported numbers are strong enough to be worth taking seriously.

Kumo Relational is a pre-trained foundation model that operates directly on a database rather than on a flattened table. You describe what you want to predict, it gathers up to **10,000 historical examples** as context, and returns a prediction in a single forward pass. No task-specific training, no feature engineering, no aggregation by hand.

## The Benchmark Claims

Across **41 tasks on 15 relational databases** — RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT and 4DBInfer, none of which were seen during pre-training — the model beats the strongest supervised baselines in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On RelBench V1 classification, it outperforms gradient-boosted trees on hand-built features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 after fine-tuning, and surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% MRR — a gap that widens to 16% with fine-tuning.

The efficiency result may matter more than the accuracy result. On the RelArena-α leaderboard, Kumo Relational sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front at roughly 17 seconds of median inference per 1,000 samples, at an Elo of 1,842. The highest-scoring entry reaches Elo 1,878 — about 36 points better — but takes some 7,300 seconds. That is roughly **430 times slower** for a margin most production pipelines would never notice.

The model also degrades gracefully: it holds performance with as little as 0.2% of the training data used as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely notices noisy columns.

## How It Works

Pre-training is entirely synthetic, built on PluRel, a relational data generator from the same team. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the underlying paper reports that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real data. At inference, a lightweight network reasons within tables via alternating column and row attention, and a larger network distributes row embeddings across the schema using graph attention over primary/foreign-key links — working on row embeddings rather than every cell, which is what keeps the cost from going quadratic.

Tasks are written in NVIDIA's Predictive Query Language, a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks the model replays historical database states and serves only pre-anchor data, which prevents leakage — the kind of detail that quietly breaks most tabular evaluations.

## Where It Still Loses

NVIDIA is candid: the approach works best where relationships and temporal dynamics carry signal, and on tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models can still edge out in-context prediction. Predictive signals also have to be reachable within a limited number of hops, so queries should start narrow. It ships through NVIDIA's open-source GPU-native `structured-data-models` library or as an NIM, and a custom graph engine handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s.

The strategic signal is bigger than the model: XGBoost pipelines are being treated as the incumbent to displace, not the baseline to improve on.
